newsitem.title: KENYA: WFP says Somali harvest better but appeals for aid.
newsitem.headline: WFP says Somali harvest better but appeals for aid.

text.p: Low cereal stocks in war-torn Somalia have been bolstered by a good harvest despite capricious weather, the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said on Sunday in an appeal for $12 million in food aid.

"Overall cereal production for this cropping season has been estimated at 242,000 tonnes. This is 37 percent lower than the pre-war average (1982/88 average of 382,953 tonnes) -- but a 58 percent increase when compared with 1995," the WFP report said.
The 1995 harvest was the worst in five years, WFP expert said.

An estimated 300,000 people died in the famine which devastated Somalia between 1991 and late 1992, when the United States sent in thousands of troops to back a U.N. operation to ensure food distribution. The last U.N. forces were withdrawn in March 1995.

WFP said it was asking donors to provide an initial $12 million for food aid for "immediate emergency assistance" to vulnerable communities, and for food-for-work projects geared toward flood protection and emergency prevention.

The report said that in 1996 severe floods and drought in some parts of Somalia caused heavy crop losses -- especially in the Lower and Middle Juba Valley, where entire communities planted two or three times without success.
The WFP agronomists were reporting after completing an assessment of Somalia's main growing season which normally accounts for 75-80 percent of total cereal production.

In the Bay region, Somalia's main bread basket where some 35 percent of the country's cereals are grown, production tripled over last year. Farmers made tremendous efforts to maximise on good and well-distributed rains by planting and cultivating as much land as possible, WFP reported.

In urban areas of Somalia such as Mogadishu and Kismayu the harvest has started to filter to markets which should lower consumer prices. But insecurity in Mogadishu continues to hinder relief agency efforts to monitor the trend of malnutrition amongst children, the agency said.
"We are not getting reports of starvation but there are more and more kids showing up at feeding centres every day," Gerard Van Dijk, WFP country director for Somalia, said.

"We're hoping that malnutrition rates will improve with more food available in the markets...But we also know that many people, especially the unemployed, will still struggle because they do not have money to buy food for their families."
Somalia has had no government since 1991 when the ouster of dictator Mohamed Siad Barre was followed by a bitter civil war.
